data.title: Amazon discloses $80 billion loan facility as AI infrastructure spending rises
data.description:
Amazon has disclosed a new loan facility that allows it to borrow up to $80 billion to purchase technology infrastructure assets. The financing arrangement comes as the company increases spending on cloud computing and AI infrastructure.

According to Amazon’s third-quarter filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the facility forms part of its supplier financing arrangements for technology infrastructure purchases. The company can access the funds at its discretion between the first quarter of 2027 and the third quarter of 2028.

The amount available will depend on the timing and extent of purchase orders, as well as pricing terms. Borrowings will carry variable interest rates and mature five years after each withdrawal.

Amazon will provide security interests in certain assets purchased through the facility, with outstanding borrowings recorded as long-term debt on its balance sheet. The filing does not specify which infrastructure assets will be purchased or identify the lenders involved.

The facility provides for potential borrowings of up to approximately $80 billion rather than funds Amazon has already drawn.

Amazon’s infrastructure spending

Amazon’s latest financial results also showed higher capital expenditure, primarily driven by investments in technology infrastructure.

Amazon reported cash capital expenditure of $75.9 billion in the third quarter of 2026, compared with $34.2 billion during the same period last year. Spending for the first nine months of 2026 reached $172.2 billion, up from $89.9 billion in the corresponding period of 2025.

The company said the expenditure primarily reflected investments in technology infrastructure, most of which supported the growth of AWS, alongside additional capacity for its fulfilment network.

Amazon expects cash capital expenditure to reach approximately $220 billion for the full year. It also expects spending to increase further in 2027, primarily because of continued investments in technology infrastructure.

The increase is reflected in AWS’s infrastructure assets. According to Amazon’s SEC filing, the cloud division’s net property and equipment assets rose from $190.1 billion at the end of 2025 to $313 billion as of September 30, 2026.

AWS recorded $147.2 billion in net additions to property and equipment during the first nine months of 2026, compared with $64.8 billion a year earlier. The figures include non-cash activity, such as equipment acquired but not yet paid for, and are not equivalent to cash capital expenditure.

Amazon’s infrastructure costs include servers, networking equipment, data centre depreciation and amortisation, rent, and utilities associated with AWS and other Amazon businesses. The company said higher infrastructure spending, including depreciation and amortisation, was the main reason technology and infrastructure costs increased during the quarter.

AWS’s depreciation and amortisation expenses reached $9.23 billion in the third quarter, up from $5.65 billion a year earlier. For the first nine months of 2026, these expenses increased to $24.6 billion from $14.9 billion in the corresponding period last year.

Amazon also reported approximately $883.6 billion in contractual commitments as of September 30, 2026. These included $159.6 billion in property and equipment commitments and $164.9 billion in leases that had not yet commenced.

These commitments cover multiple years and business activities, not just AWS. Amazon’s filing also disclosed purchasing arrangements that allow the company to defer payments for certain technology infrastructure assets for up to one year.

Higher capital expenditure has also affected Amazon’s cash flow. The company reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, compared with positive free cash flow of $14.8 billion a year earlier.

Amazon attributed the decline primarily to a $94.8 billion year-on-year increase in purchases of property and equipment, net of proceeds from sales and incentives, mainly related to AI investments.

AWS growth and financing

AWS reported revenue of $46 billion in the third quarter of 2026, an increase of 39.3% from the previous year. According to Amazon, this was the cloud division’s fastest revenue growth in nearly five years.

Operating income for AWS increased to $17.8 billion from $11.4 billion a year earlier. Amazon attributed the revenue increase primarily to higher customer usage, partially offset by pricing changes associated with long-term customer contracts.

During Amazon’s third-quarter earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy discussed the pace of the company’s AI infrastructure deployment.

“We’re installing an AI accelerator about every 14 seconds,” Jassy said, adding that customers were using the new capacity almost as quickly as AWS installed it.

Jassy also reported that Amazon’s chip business continued to record triple-digit year-on-year percentage growth, while revenue commitments for its Graviton processors and Trainium AI accelerators had each increased more than twentyfold.

“Our Chips business continues to grow triple digit percentages year over year,” Jassy said during the earnings call.

Amazon has not specified whether its custom AI accelerators will be financed through the new $80 billion facility.

Amazon has also secured financing through other borrowing arrangements in 2026. These include a $17.5 billion unsecured term loan agreed in June and drawn in September, alongside bond issuances denominated in US dollars and several other currencies.

The new $80 billion facility differs from these unsecured borrowing arrangements because Amazon will provide security interests in certain infrastructure assets purchased through it.

As of September 30, 2026, Amazon reported $173.1 billion in long-term debt on its balance sheet, compared with $65.6 billion at the end of 2025.

data.title: Microsoft reviews neocloud deals amid AI data centre delays
data.description:
Microsoft is tightening oversight of data centre projects involving specialist cloud providers as construction delays, rising costs, and regulatory issues affect infrastructure delivery.

According to Bloomberg, the company is reviewing projects involving Nebius, IREN, and Nscale. Citing people familiar with the matter, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is stepping away from projects it considers too risky and internally discussing whether to sign additional agreements with neocloud providers.

Microsoft is also placing greater emphasis on developing its own data centres while continuing to use external providers for additional cloud and AI computing capacity.

In comments reported by Reuters, Microsoft said its infrastructure strategy combines company-owned data centres, leased facilities, and partnerships with external providers. The company has not announced plans to discontinue its use of third-party infrastructure.

Microsoft faces delays in third-party capacity deliveries

Microsoft disclosed delays in third-party infrastructure deliveries during its latest quarterly earnings announcement, before Bloomberg reported on the company’s review of neocloud projects.

During its fiscal first-quarter earnings call, Microsoft reported capital expenditure of $45.2 billion for the quarter ended September 30, 2026.

“Some third-party capacity deliveries we expected in Q1 were delayed,” CFO Amy Hood said during the earnings call, explaining the timing of the company’s infrastructure spending.

Approximately three-quarters of Microsoft’s capital expenditure went towards shorter-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs. The remaining expenditure covered longer-lived infrastructure assets, including data centres.

Microsoft expects capital expenditure to exceed $50 billion in its fiscal second quarter. Hood said some third-party capacity deliveries had shifted into the second half of the fiscal year.

The company also expects spending to accelerate during that period, partly because of the rescheduled infrastructure deliveries. Microsoft projected capital expenditure of approximately $170 billion for calendar year 2026.

Microsoft has continued developing its own infrastructure alongside third-party projects. During the same earnings call, CEO Satya Nadella said the company added 24 data centres across five continents during the quarter.

Microsoft scales back Nscale expansion plans

Microsoft has decided not to exercise an option to expand its computing capacity agreement with UK-based Nscale at a separate site in Ward County, Texas, according to Reuters and the Financial Times.

The companies announced an expanded agreement in October 2025 covering approximately 200,000 Nvidia GB300 GPUs across facilities in Europe and the United States. Nscale’s original announcement included plans to deploy approximately 104,000 GPUs at a 240-megawatt (MW) facility in Ward County.

Nscale’s existing Texas deployment is located at a site leased from Ionic Digital. Microsoft also held an option to secure additional computing capacity at a separate Nscale-owned site nearby.

The proposed expansion involved approximately 500 MW of additional capacity. Microsoft decided not to proceed with the option amid difficulties securing the necessary electricity supply arrangements for the project.

Nscale corrected its October 2025 announcement on November 5, removing an earlier statement that Microsoft held a 700 MW expansion option. The correction did not remove the company’s separate claim that the existing Texas campus had the potential to scale to 700 MW.

A person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Microsoft made its decision several months before Nscale filed for its initial public offering in September 2026. The decision did not affect the existing Texas agreement or Nscale’s approximately $103 billion in disclosed contracted business across its operations.

Microsoft also withdrew from an agreement to become an anchor customer at Nscale’s proposed data centre in Loughton, Essex. The withdrawal followed delays to the site’s power connection, which pushed the expected electricity supply date into the 2030s.

IREN reports delays to Microsoft infrastructure deliveries

IREN, another provider working with Microsoft, has postponed deliveries of some AI infrastructure following changes to network designs requested by the software company.

The companies signed a five-year GPU cloud services agreement in November 2025, with a total contract value of approximately $9.7 billion. The agreement includes a 20% customer prepayment and provides Microsoft with access to Nvidia GB300 GPUs.

IREN also entered into an agreement with Dell Technologies to purchase approximately $5.8 billion worth of GPUs and associated equipment for the deployment. The infrastructure is being installed at IREN’s Childress campus in Texas, with deliveries scheduled in phases.

The project comprises four Horizon data centres designed to support a combined 200 MW of critical IT capacity. Each facility is designed to provide approximately 50 MW of capacity, with liquid cooling used to support high-density GPU deployments.

IREN said the first Horizon facility entered service for Microsoft during the quarter ended September 30, while the remaining three facilities had reached late-stage construction.

In its earnings announcement, IREN revised its target for reaching more than $4 billion in annualised run-rate revenue from the end of 2026 to January 2027, with a possible extension to the end of February.

“The more than $4 billion of contracted ARR is funded and now targeted for January,” IREN co-founder and co-CEO Daniel Roberts said in the announcement, attributing the revised schedule to a customer-requested design change and supplier timing issues.

The target covers IREN’s broader AI cloud operations rather than revenue from Microsoft alone. The figure is based on contracted GPU capacity and pricing and is not equivalent to revenue already recognised under accounting standards.

According to Reuters, IREN will not incur financial penalties for delays arising from Microsoft’s requested network design changes. The company has not announced any cancellation of its Microsoft agreement.

IREN also reported approximately $15 billion in remaining planned capital expenditure for fiscal year 2027. Of that amount, $9 billion is expected to be covered by cash, committed GPU financing, and customer prepayments.

The remaining $6 billion is expected to come from additional GPU financing, customer prepayments, data centre financing, and other corporate funding sources, subject to market conditions.

data.title: Microsoft licensing rules influence Azure cloud decisions, survey finds
data.description:
Microsoft’s software licensing rules are influencing cloud provider decisions among surveyed US businesses, according to findings from 410 software and cloud decision-makers.

The survey, conducted for the Coalition for Fair Software Licensing (CFSL), found that 83% of respondents said Microsoft’s licensing rules meaningfully affected their choice of cloud provider. Among organisations that considered alternatives to Microsoft Azure, 61% ultimately selected Azure to avoid additional licensing fees.

In a hypothetical scenario where licensing restrictions were removed and costs were not a factor, eight in ten respondents said they would move workloads away from Azure, according to the survey.

Licensing costs affect cloud migration decisions

The survey also reported financial consequences for businesses affected by higher licensing costs. Among those businesses, 56% said they had increased prices for customers to cover the additional expenses, while the same proportion reported cutting spending in other areas.

Nearly two-thirds of respondents said their organisations had kept at least one workload on their own servers rather than moving it to the cloud because of licensing restrictions.

“Businesses are being steered to Azure by financial penalties rather than by merit,” Ryan Triplette, executive director of the CFSL, said.

The findings reflect the responses of 410 US software and cloud decision-makers and do not necessarily represent the experiences of Microsoft’s wider enterprise customer base.

Microsoft’s licensing documentation outlines different conditions for deploying existing software licences across cloud providers, depending on the product, licensing agreement, and hosting environment.

Under Microsoft’s Flexible Virtualization Benefit, customers with eligible subscriptions or active Software Assurance can deploy Windows Server and certain other Microsoft software on shared or dedicated infrastructure operated by authorised outsourcers.

However, the benefit excludes Microsoft’s designated Listed Providers, which include Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google, Alibaba, and Microsoft itself. Microsoft also states that Windows Server is not eligible for its separate License Mobility through Software Assurance programme, although customers can obtain Windows Server licensing through other cloud arrangements.

Microsoft’s documentation also specifies different deployment rights for certain licences acquired before October 1, 2019.

UK regulator examines Microsoft’s licensing practices

Microsoft’s licensing practices are also under regulatory scrutiny in the UK, where the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is examining the company’s position in the business software market.

On October 16, the CMA proposed designating Microsoft with strategic market status under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024. The designation would allow the regulator to consider targeted measures addressing competition concerns.

In its provisional findings, the CMA identified barriers to switching providers and commercial practices that reinforce Microsoft’s position in business software. The regulator is also examining whether customers have sufficient choice over which cloud platforms they use to deploy existing software licences.

The proposal remains subject to consultation and does not establish wrongdoing. The CMA is seeking feedback before deciding whether Microsoft meets the criteria for strategic market status.

Microsoft disagreed with the CMA’s assessment. “All our products — including Copilot — are open and interoperable,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in a statement reported by Reuters. The company maintained that customers could use its products alongside competing services.

Microsoft also welcomed the CMA’s acknowledgement that its position in cloud services did not warrant a separate strategic market status designation.

The regulator is accepting responses to its consultation until November 13, 2026, and must issue its final designation decision by February 13, 2027.

CMA pushes for greater multicloud flexibility

In a separate effort to address cloud switching barriers, the CMA has been working with Microsoft and AWS on measures intended to give businesses more flexibility when moving workloads or using multiple cloud providers.

In its October 16 update, the regulator reported progress on these measures, including removing data transfer fees for customers changing providers and reducing charges for organisations using multiple cloud platforms.

The measures also cover direct connectivity between competing cloud providers’ data centres and processes for customers and competitors to request improvements to interoperability.

However, the CMA said further work was needed to address identity and access management across cloud environments and technical barriers to migrating applications designed for portability.

The CMA plans to continue monitoring cloud portability measures and publish another update in spring 2027.

data.title: Nvidia reportedly limits Chinese access to overseas AI cloud services
data.description:
Nvidia has reportedly asked its cloud computing partners to reduce their business with Chinese customers, directing them to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, the instructions were issued in recent months, citing five people familiar with the matter. They were communicated verbally through Nvidia’s sales staff and regional teams rather than through formal written policies, and apply only to future contracts. Existing agreements remain unaffected.

The Information separately reported that the guidance is not mandatory and has not been strictly enforced. The publication also said Nvidia was encouraging cloud providers, including Nvidia-backed neocloud operators, to diversify their customer base and identify the end users accessing its chips.

Nvidia has not publicly explained how the reported 51% requirement would be calculated or monitored.

US export controls address overseas GPU access

The reported instructions come amid US restrictions on China’s access to advanced semiconductors used in AI development. Since 2022, Washington has introduced export controls limiting shipments of certain Nvidia processors to China.

Chinese technology companies have also accessed advanced computing resources through overseas cloud providers, allowing them to rent GPU capacity without importing the hardware. These arrangements provide access to Nvidia-powered infrastructure for AI workloads, including model training.

In May 2025, the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a policy statement identifying circumstances in which exports or transfers of advanced computing chips to foreign infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) providers could require an export licence.

Under the guidance, licensing requirements can apply when exporters know that hardware supplied to foreign cloud providers will be used to train AI models for or on behalf of entities headquartered in China or other designated countries of concern, where the activity involves weapons of mass destruction or military-intelligence end uses or end users. The policy addresses specific activities rather than imposing a blanket prohibition on Chinese companies accessing overseas cloud services.

Separate BIS guidance issued in May 2025 recommended that semiconductor suppliers verify customer identities, ownership structures, and the intended use of advanced computing hardware. It also identified data centre inspections, end-user certifications, and independent audits as measures to prevent chips from reaching restricted entities.

BIS also recommended additional scrutiny of data centres with infrastructure capable of operating servers containing advanced computing chips at more than 10 megawatts. The agency said facilities at this scale can provide access to large amounts of computing capacity for AI model training.

US officials have also examined Chinese AI companies’ access to Nvidia chips through overseas data centres. One reported case involved Moonshot AI, the developer of the Kimi AI model, following allegations that the company had used Nvidia processors housed outside China.

Nvidia tightens checks on Asian cloud providers

Nvidia had previously tightened its screening of Asian customers. In July, the Financial Times reported that the company had removed more than half of its previously approved Asian buyers from a list of companies authorised to purchase its AI chips, with smaller GPU cloud providers among those affected.

The stricter compliance checks were intended to prevent advanced US semiconductors from reaching China through third countries. According to the report, Nvidia increased its due diligence procedures in Singapore, Malaysia, and Japan, including visits to customer data centres, contract verification, and interviews with end users.

Companies that failed the initial reviews were reportedly removed from the approved customer list but could reapply after addressing compliance deficiencies.

The reported 51% requirement has raised concerns among cloud providers operating Nvidia-powered infrastructure. According to the Financial Times, some operators have warned that securing enough non-Chinese customers would be difficult, particularly outside the US.

A Singapore-based cloud provider told the publication that strict enforcement would hurt its business. Other operators reportedly warned that they might have to reduce operations if they could not attract enough customers outside China.

Some overseas data centre operators have also begun seeking additional non-Chinese customers in response to the reported instructions, according to the Financial Times.

Nvidia has not publicly confirmed or denied the reported customer allocation requirement. In a statement provided to AFP, the company addressed the role of US computing infrastructure in the global AI market.

“Data centres and clouds built on American chips are the foundation that American model and application makers need to compete worldwide,” Nvidia said.

The company added that longstanding US policy encourages cloud providers to build on American infrastructure and seek customers internationally.

(Photo by Brecht Corbeel)
data.author: Muhammad Zulhusni

data.title: AWS brings native PyTorch support to Trainium chips with TorchNeuron
data.description:
AWS has introduced TorchNeuron, an open-source software tool that allows developers to run existing PyTorch applications on its Trainium AI chips with minimal code changes. The tool supports AI training and inference workloads through PyTorch’s native programming interfaces.

TorchNeuron is scheduled to enter public beta on October 20 during the PyTorch Conference North America. The software supports AWS Trainium2 and Trainium3 chips and is being released under the Apache 2.0 open-source licence.

Native PyTorch support expands Trainium compatibility

TorchNeuron integrates with PyTorch through its existing hardware extension system, allowing developers to use Trainium through standard programming interfaces. Developers can select Trainium by changing the device setting in their code to neuron, while applications using supported hardware-independent PyTorch interfaces can run without changes to their model code.

PyTorch already supports Nvidia GPUs through CUDA, which provides access to Nvidia’s computing libraries and development tools. TorchNeuron extends native PyTorch support to AWS Trainium through the framework’s PrivateUse1 hardware extension mechanism.

“Developers should have a consistent experience across hardware platforms,” Jana van Greunen, director of PyTorch engineering at Meta, said. The integration allows developers to use existing PyTorch development and distributed training interfaces on supported Trainium hardware.

TorchNeuron supports PyTorch’s eager execution mode, allowing developers to debug individual operations using standard Python tools. It also supports torch.compile, which optimises model operations for Trainium hardware.

The software supports distributed training through standard PyTorch interfaces, including Fully Sharded Data Parallelism 2 (FSDP2), DistributedDataParallel, tensor parallelism, and pipeline parallelism. These capabilities allow developers to distribute training workloads across multiple Trainium accelerators and servers.

Developers can also use Neuron Explorer alongside the standard PyTorch profiler to examine hardware activity, identify performance bottlenecks, and trace operations back to their source code. The Neuron Kernel Interface provides additional control by allowing developers to create custom operations for specific workloads.

Hugging Face has added native TorchNeuron support to its Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT, and TRL libraries. Previously, supported Trainium workloads relied on the separate XLA-based Optimum Neuron integration, which used specialised model classes and training tools.

The new integration allows developers to use standard Hugging Face model definitions and training scripts on Trainium. Hugging Face said TorchNeuron supports 89% of the 100 most-used text-generation model architectures, compared with 46% under Optimum Neuron version 0.4.5.

The figures measure model architecture compatibility rather than inference performance. Developers can load supported models onto Trainium using the device_map=”neuron” setting, while Diffusers also supports image and video generation workloads.

Hugging Face said the new integration allows developers to save trained models using standard Transformers checkpoints. These checkpoints can be uploaded to the Hugging Face Hub and loaded on other supported hardware.

Early performance results and technical limitations

AWS and PyTorch have published examples of organisations testing TorchNeuron for AI inference workloads, including speech AI companies Deepgram and Cartesia. The deployments demonstrate how the software has been used with existing PyTorch applications.

Deepgram worked with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center over several months to move its model to native PyTorch on Trainium. The company reported improved cost performance compared with its existing GPU systems.

“In the benchmarks we evaluated, Trainium processes about 60% more input audio seconds per dollar than our existing GPU baselines,” Adam Sypniewski, CTO of Deepgram, said.

The result reflects Deepgram’s evaluated speech AI workloads rather than a general performance comparison between Trainium and GPU-based cloud instances.

Voice AI company Cartesia also tested TorchNeuron with its existing inference pipeline. According to the company, its engineers were able to run standard PyTorch code on Trainium with minimal changes, while using custom kernels to optimise operations that have a greater effect on processing latency.

TorchNeuron remains in public beta and does not yet support every PyTorch operation. According to AWS documentation, native dynamic shape support is still under development, while APIs such as torch.sparse, torch.func, and torch.nested remain unsupported.

The current release also requires dynamic=False when using torch.compile, and different input shapes can require separate compilations. AWS recommends grouping or padding inputs to reduce repeated compilation.

Unsupported operations can fall back to CPU execution in eager mode, potentially affecting performance. Developers can use TorchNeuron’s profiling tools to identify these operations and other performance bottlenecks.

TorchNeuron is being distributed through the AWS Neuron software stack for compatible Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. Its open-source implementation is available through AWS’s GitHub repository under the Apache 2.0 licence.
data.author: Muhammad Zulhusni

data.title: Building an ERP system around your processes, not the other way around
data.description:
Lidl spent an estimated €500 million over seven years trying to move its merchandise management onto SAP before halting the project in 2018.

The sticking point was mundane. Lidl valued its inventory at purchase prices, while the standard retail software worked from retail prices, and the company would not give up a method it saw as part of its edge. So the software was adapted instead, and the adaptations slowed the system and pushed up its cost.

The lesson usually drawn from the story is “never customise.” A better one is that a company with a genuinely different process should not be bending a package designed around somebody else’s. Telling those two situations apart early is the real work behind process-first design, and it is why Crunch-IS is a leader in ERP development services. It starts long before anyone writes code.

The mismatch is already on record

In a 2023 survey of 251 technology leaders, 73% said their organization’s ERP strategy was not strongly aligned with its business strategy. Panorama Consulting’s implementation data tells the same story from the other side. Between 2013 and 2016, the share of companies that went live with no customisation at all never rose above 12%.

Few organisations use ERP software entirely out of the box. The real question is not whether to customise it, but how much customisation is justified, what it will cost, and whether the decisions are driven by a clear business strategy.

The real process lives in spreadsheets

Ask a finance team how budgeting works and you will hear about the ERP. Watch them do it and you will see Excel. A PayEm survey of 270 finance professionals, published in November 2024, found that 86% still rely on Excel for budgeting and forecasting.

Writing for CFO Dive in 2025, a Gartner senior director noted that 51% of finance leaders still choose a detailed bottom-up planning process built in spreadsheets, then load the results into their planning system.

Those spreadsheets are the most accurate process documentation most companies own. They show the approval that happens by email, the margin check someone runs by hand every Friday, and the customer who always gets special terms.

An ERP project that ignores the spreadsheets will replicate the official process and lose the one people actually follow. Before design starts, collect every spreadsheet that feeds a monthly decision and ask who would complain if it disappeared. The answers tell you which logic the new system has to carry.

Sorting processes into three piles

Process-first does not mean building everything from scratch. It means deciding, process-by-process, which of three treatments each one deserves:

  • Commodity processes. General ledger, payroll, tax, and fixed assets work roughly the same way everywhere, and regulators like it that way. Adopt the standard and stop debating.
  • Differentiating processes. Lidl’s inventory valuation was one. So is a manufacturer’s own scheduling logic, or a distributor’s rebate model built up over twenty years of customer deals. Build around these deliberately, with their own data model, rather than as patches on someone else’s.
  • Broken processes. Some workflows exist only because the old system could not do better. Five sign-offs on a routine stationery order are not a competitive advantage. Fix these before automating them, or the new ERP will run the waste faster.

A quick test for the second pile: would a customer, supplier, or regulator notice if the process changed tomorrow? If nobody outside the building would, it probably belongs in the first pile, however attached the team is to it. Most companies find the second pile is smaller than they expected and the third is larger.

Map the work before you model the data

Panorama’s survey of 140 organisations that implemented ERP in 2021 found that 52% sought outside help with business process management and reengineering, while only 27% did so for digital strategy. The instinct is right. The execution is often thin, because process mapping gets compressed into a few workshops where managers describe how things should work.

Better inputs are cheap. System logs show what actually happens and in what order. Shadowing a buyer for two days shows the workarounds no one mentions in a meeting. The exception queue shows where the current process breaks. A data model drawn from those sources holds up in testing. One drawn from a workshop whiteboard usually doesn’t.

Sometimes the business should change

Process-first has limits, and Nike found them. In 2000, its new i2 demand-planning system misfired and the company later tied about $100 million in lost sales to the problem. Its stock fell roughly 20%.

i2 argued that the trouble came from Nike’s customised implementation rather than the software. Nike eventually moved short- and medium-range planning into its SAP ERP.

Write the process down first
data.author: Ryan Daws

data.title: Malaysia develops sovereign AI cloud to protect government data
data.description:
Malaysia is developing a sovereign AI cloud to strengthen protection of classified government information amid concerns over foreign data access laws.

Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil confirmed on October 14 that implementation was underway and that the initiative would be managed by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) and the Communications Ministry, according to Bernama.

Fahmi raised concerns about the security of classified information stored with public cloud providers subject to foreign legislation. “We have observed that some countries have policies and laws that could make the use of public clouds less secure,” Fahmi said.

Malaysia outlines RM2 billion sovereign AI cloud investment

The initiative was included in Budget 2026, with the government proposing an RM2 billion investment through MCMC. According to the Ministry of Digital, the investment is intended to fund infrastructure for protecting national data and supporting large-scale AI applications.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced plans for the Sovereign AI Cloud in October 2025, following discussions at the National Digital Economy and Fourth Industrial Revolution Council. The infrastructure is intended to support government services and Malaysia’s national AI capabilities.

In October 2025, Fahmi said MCMC would implement the project with guidance from the National Security Council, Ministry of Digital, and National Digital Department. He also said the initiative would strengthen protections for strategic government information, including classified material covered by Malaysia’s Official Secrets Act.

The announcements reviewed do not identify the cloud infrastructure providers, technical architecture, computing capacity, or deployment timeline for the project. They also do not specify which government applications will be hosted on the platform.

Foreign data access laws shape cloud policy

The government’s concerns over foreign jurisdiction were raised before the Sovereign AI Cloud was announced. In September 2025, Fahmi cited the United States’ Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act (CLOUD Act) while the government was examining the need for a sovereign cloud policy.

Under the CLOUD Act, service providers subject to US jurisdiction can be required through lawful processes to disclose data in their possession, custody, or control, regardless of where it is stored.

Fahmi said Malaysia needed to examine cloud security requirements to protect sensitive and classified information. At the time, the government had not reached a final decision on a separate sovereign cloud policy.

Separately, Malaysia launched its National Cloud Computing Policy (NCCP) in August 2025 to guide cloud adoption across the public and private sectors. The policy addresses public sector cloud adoption, data protection, privacy, and compliance with relevant security and regulatory requirements.

The announcements reviewed have not detailed the data residency arrangements, access controls, or operational safeguards that will be used for the Sovereign AI Cloud.

data.title: AWS faces cloud capacity crunch as AI demand stretches into 2028
data.description:
AWS has largely booked its computing capacity for major customer commitments in 2027, with some commitments extending into 2028, according to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy.

Speaking on the a16z Show podcast on October 23, Jassy said AWS was struggling to meet demand from AI developers and enterprise customers despite Amazon’s plans to spend approximately $220 billion on capital expenditure in 2026.

“2027 is largely sold out,” Jassy said, adding that “a good chunk of 2028 is sold out.” The company’s capacity for 2026 has also been fully committed, excluding resources reserved for on-demand services.

Jassy clarified that the commitments primarily concern large allocations of computing capacity rather than all AWS services. The company continues to reserve resources for on-demand workloads through Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) and its managed generative AI service, Amazon Bedrock.

Amazon has not disclosed the exact amount of computing capacity committed for 2027 and 2028 or how much remains available for on-demand customers.

AWS faces infrastructure and capacity planning challenges

Jassy identified data centre availability, electricity, and memory supply as constraints on AWS’s ability to expand computing capacity. He said shortages affecting different infrastructure components would continue beyond 2027.

Memory shortages are also affecting how AWS allocates resources between AI and conventional cloud workloads. AI accelerators use high-bandwidth memory (HBM), while conventional servers typically rely on other forms of dynamic random-access memory (DRAM).

Jassy said AWS faces allocation decisions as demand for both AI and non-AI computing services increases.

During Amazon’s second-quarter 2026 earnings call, Jassy said data centre spending typically begins about two years before servers can be put into service. Servers and networking equipment are generally purchased only a few months before they are needed.

This allows AWS to reduce equipment purchases if customer demand falls short of expectations. Its data centre infrastructure, meanwhile, is designed to remain operational for more than 30 years.

AWS’s infrastructure spending is partly supported by long-term customer agreements. In Amazon’s 2025 shareholder letter, Jassy said the company had secured commitments covering a substantial portion of its planned 2026 AWS investment.

One example is AWS’s agreement with OpenAI, which was expanded by $100 billion over eight years in the first quarter of 2026. The expansion added to an existing $38 billion multi-year arrangement, bringing the combined commitment to approximately $138 billion.

According to Amazon’s regulatory filing, the agreement includes contractual obligations related to the performance of AWS chips.

Jassy said much of the AWS infrastructure spending planned for 2026 was expected to generate revenue in 2027 and 2028.

Amazon’s second-quarter regulatory filing disclosed approximately $496 billion in remaining performance obligations as of June 30, 2026, primarily related to AWS customer contracts with original terms exceeding one year. These obligations represent future contracted services that have not yet been recognised as revenue.

The company reported a weighted-average remaining life of 6.4 years for its long-term contracts. The $496 billion figure does not represent the amount of computing capacity physically reserved by customers.

During Amazon’s second-quarter earnings call, Jassy said most AI computing capacity was being contracted for at least five years. Investments in servers and networking equipment typically take slightly less than three years to break even, while the equipment has an expected useful life of at least five to six years.

Amazon raised its 2026 capital expenditure forecast from approximately $200 billion to $220 billion during its second-quarter earnings call in July, partly because of higher memory costs. The company said the spending would primarily support AI infrastructure, alongside investments in other operations, including robotics, semiconductors, and satellites.

Despite the increased investment, Jassy said AWS continued to face more demand than it could accommodate. He said Amazon could spend considerably more on infrastructure without fully satisfying customer requirements.

How AWS is managing cloud capacity for customers

During the podcast, Jassy also addressed how AWS balances demand from AI companies with the requirements of existing enterprise customers.

Asked whether AWS would prioritise AI developers willing to pay higher prices over established customers running conventional cloud workloads, Jassy rejected the idea of diverting capacity away from those customers.

“We’re not going to squeeze our customers,” Jassy said.

He added that AWS would continue supporting customers running their core applications while expanding capacity for AI workloads.

AWS offers capacity reservation services for customers with scheduled computing requirements. EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservations allow businesses to reserve specific instance capacity within an Availability Zone, including eligible future-dated reservations.

Customers can request future-dated Capacity Reservations between five and 120 days in advance. AWS assesses requests based on factors including forecast capacity availability, reservation size, and commitment duration.

AWS also offers EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML, which allow customers to reserve GPU-based computing resources for scheduled workloads. The service supports AI model training, fine-tuning, and inference, with availability depending on the requested instance type, location, and reservation period.

These services provide ways to secure computing resources ahead of planned deployments once reservations are confirmed. However, AWS has not disclosed how much capacity remains available through these services or how its long-term AI commitments affect availability for other customers.

data.title: Google Cloud outage disrupts UK banks as regulators seek answers
data.description:
European financial regulators have contacted Google following a cloud outage that disrupted banking services across the UK and Europe on October 20. The incident affected financial institutions including Revolut, Lloyds Banking Group, and HSBC, with customers reporting problems accessing banking services.

The European Banking Authority (EBA) told Reuters it had contacted Google Cloud to gather information about the disruption and assess its potential impact on financial institutions operating in the European Union.

The outage has also drawn attention from UK authorities, with Parliament’s Treasury Committee seeking information from the Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) about their response.

Google Cloud outage affects banking services

The disruption began at 06:08 UTC on October 20 after a power event affected Google’s europe-west2-b availability zone in London. The failure also caused elevated error rates and intermittent network issues across the wider europe-west2 region, according to Google’s service health dashboard.

Google’s incident report listed 38 affected services, including Google Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Storage. Some workloads became unavailable, while customers using other services experienced errors and network connectivity problems.

Google advised affected customers to migrate workloads to another available zone or region where feasible. The company also prioritised restoring existing workloads, while some customers remained temporarily unable to create new ones.

Google recorded the incident between 06:08 and 14:00 UTC, although recovery was not simultaneous across all affected services. The company reported that services for most workloads were recovering by 12:10 UTC. By its final update at 14:03 UTC, Google said the issue had been mitigated for most customers, with a very small number still affected.

A Google spokesperson confirmed that the disruption involved a power event at a third-party facility supporting its London cloud region, according to Reuters. “Services have been restored. We will update our public status dashboard with an analysis,” the Google spokesperson said.

The disruption affected several banking services, with Revolut reporting problems involving account logins, card payments, cash withdrawals, and transfers. Lloyds and HSBC also reported difficulties affecting their digital banking services.

Revolut, which serves approximately 13 million customers in the UK, said customer funds and data remained secure throughout the incident. The company also said it was reviewing the disruption to reduce the impact of similar third-party service failures.

Regulators examine cloud resilience requirements

The outage occurred just over three months after the UK began directly overseeing four critical technology providers serving its financial sector. Google Cloud EMEA Limited, Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited, and Oracle Corporation UK Limited came under the new oversight arrangements on July 13th.

The Bank of England, Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA), and FCA jointly oversee the resilience of critical services provided by these companies. The regime requires designated providers to manage risks affecting their services, conduct resilience testing, and report major operational incidents.

The Bank of England said the framework addresses risks arising when multiple financial institutions rely on the same technology provider. The central bank warned that disruption at a widely used provider can affect several financial institutions or markets simultaneously, potentially affecting financial stability and services used by consumers and businesses.

Google Cloud EMEA Limited was also among 19 critical information and communications technology (ICT) third-party providers designated under the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) in November 2025. The designation considers a provider’s importance to financial institutions, its role in supporting critical functions, and the availability of alternative services.

Under DORA, the EBA, European Securities and Markets Authority, and European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority oversee designated critical ICT providers through a Lead Overseer framework. The responsible authority can request information, conduct investigations and inspections, and issue recommendations concerning risks associated with services supplied to financial institutions.

Reuters reported on October 21 that the EBA had contacted Google Cloud to obtain further information about the incident and assess its implications for financial institutions in the EU. The report did not indicate that the regulator had initiated formal enforcement action against Google.

UK lawmakers have also requested more information about the disruption. Treasury Committee Chair Dame Meg Hillier wrote to the Bank of England and FCA on October 20, seeking details about the outage’s cause, the number of affected financial institutions and consumers, and the regulators’ response.

The committee also asked whether customers suffered financial losses and what lessons the incident offers for the operational resilience of both cloud providers and financial institutions. It requested an initial response by November 4, followed by a full response by January 20, 2027.

The FCA separately confirmed to Reuters that it was engaging with Google over the incident. Under the UK’s critical third-party regime, designated providers are required to report major operational incidents to the relevant regulators.

The UK and EU frameworks also maintain financial institutions’ responsibility for managing their own operational resilience, even when services are outsourced to cloud providers. Banks remain responsible for managing third-party technology risks, including business continuity, recovery arrangements, and contingency planning.

UK and EU financial regulators signed a memorandum of understanding in January to coordinate oversight of critical technology providers operating across both jurisdictions. The agreement covers information sharing during operational incidents, including power outages and cyberattacks, and aims to reduce duplicated oversight.

data.title: Microsoft exits UK AI data centre deal amid reported power grid delays
data.description:
Microsoft has withdrawn from an agreement to lease computing capacity at a planned AI data centre in Loughton, Essex, operated by British cloud infrastructure provider Nscale, amid reported delays in securing electricity for the facility.

The withdrawal was first reported by The Telegraph on October 18th. According to Reuters, Microsoft recently terminated its agreement for the project, although the company has not publicly explained its decision.

The facility was intended to support Microsoft’s Azure cloud services. Nscale has maintained that it will proceed with the development despite losing its main customer.

Power delays disrupt Nscale’s data centre plans

Nscale first announced the Loughton development in January 2025, targeting the fourth quarter of 2026 for the facility to become operational. The company planned to provide an initial 50 megawatts (MW) of AI computing capacity, expandable to 90MW, using liquid cooling to support high-density GPU deployments.

In September 2025, Nscale announced an agreement with Microsoft to deploy 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs at the facility, with delivery scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. The computing infrastructure was intended to support Azure services in the UK.

However, the project has encountered delays in securing the electricity needed to operate the facility. According to The Guardian, UK Power Networks informed Nscale that sufficient power would not be available until the early to mid-2030s, several years after the originally planned opening.

Microsoft was expected to be the main customer for the Loughton facility. Its withdrawal leaves Nscale without a publicly announced replacement customer for the site, although the company has maintained that the project will proceed.

Nscale said it is examining alternative electricity sources and additional sites in the UK. The company has not provided a revised timetable for Loughton or confirmed when sufficient power will become available.

“Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term,” an Nscale spokesperson said in a statement to Reuters. The spokesperson added that the electricity grid problems would not affect the company’s other contracts with Microsoft.

Microsoft declined to comment on the reported termination.

Microsoft’s withdrawal changes Nscale’s commercial position

Microsoft had agreed to lease the initial 50MW of computing capacity at Loughton, according to the Financial Times. Its withdrawal leaves Nscale seeking another customer for the facility.

The cancellation comes after Nscale filed for a US initial public offering (IPO) in September 2026. The Nvidia-backed company disclosed details of its contracts and computing capacity in a registration statement with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).

According to the filing, Nscale had approximately $103.4 billion in active and contracted total contract value as of August 31st, up from $38 billion at the end of 2025. The agreements covered approximately 461,000 GPUs that were either active or contracted.

Of the $103.4 billion total, approximately $2.6 billion represented active contract value. Nscale also reported around 25,000 active GPUs out of 461,000 active and contracted GPUs as of August 31st.

The company said its agreements are primarily structured as long-term take-or-pay contracts, under which customers commit to paying for specified computing capacity over an agreed period.

The figures cover Nscale’s wider contract portfolio rather than revenue generated from Loughton. The company has not disclosed the value of the terminated agreement or how Microsoft’s withdrawal affects its reported contract total.

The Essex facility was also part of Microsoft’s wider AI infrastructure investment plans in the UK. In September 2025, Microsoft announced plans to invest $30 billion in the country over four years, including spending on AI infrastructure and cloud operations.

Microsoft’s relationship with Nscale also extends beyond Loughton. The companies have separate AI infrastructure agreements covering facilities in the United States, Portugal, and Norway, which Nscale said remain unaffected by the Essex project’s electricity supply problems.

Nscale has also explored on-site electricity generation and ways to accelerate access to grid power, according to The Guardian. Its September SEC filing describes behind-the-meter power infrastructure at large AI campuses, although the company has not confirmed whether such a system will be installed at Loughton.

UK seeks to reform data centre grid connections

The delays affecting Loughton come as UK energy regulator Ofgem seeks to address a backlog of electricity grid connection applications, including those from data centre developers.

In July, Ofgem reported that demand connection applications had risen from 41 gigawatts (GW) to 125GW in less than a year. Data centre projects accounted for at least 80GW of that total.

The increase occurred between November 2024 and June 2025. Ofgem said some projects in the queue might never proceed, potentially delaying developments that are ready to connect and making electricity network planning more difficult.

To address the backlog, Ofgem proposed introducing a commitment fee of between £237,500 and £712,500 per megawatt for large data centre developments accepting grid connection offers. The proposed range represents approximately 2.5% to 7.5% of average project costs.

The fee would be refunded when a project reaches energisation but forfeited if the developer exits the connection queue early. The regulator said the measure is intended to discourage speculative applications from reserving grid capacity.

Ofgem also proposed project milestones requiring developers to demonstrate progress through evidence of financial capability, commercial readiness, and equipment procurement. These requirements would apply to qualifying projects seeking to retain their position in the connection queue.

“The connections system must work for consumers and for the projects that are ready to invest, build and connect,” Eleanor Warburton, Ofgem’s director for energy system design and development, said.

The proposals form part of a wider programme involving Ofgem, the UK government, and the National Energy System Operator to reform electricity demand connections. The programme covers queue management, infrastructure planning, and measures to accelerate physical grid connections.

Ofgem has not linked the proposed reforms to Microsoft’s withdrawal from Loughton. The measures remain subject to a final regulatory decision.

Ofgem’s consultation officially closed on September 17th, with the proposed commitment fees and project requirements still awaiting a final regulatory decision.
